summary: Describes Dead Peer Detection (DPD), a method used by a number of vendors to detect a dead IKE peer. It uses IPsec traffic patterns to minimize the IKE messages needed to confirm liveness, so a router can fail over and reclaim lost resources. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If you are chatting and your friend goes quiet, you check they are still there. This lets secure tunnel gear check on its partner only when needed, and give up if nobody answers.

questions: how to detect a dead ipsec peer
why is dpd more scalable than heartbeats
subtitle: Telling when a secure tunnel peer has died without sending constant heartbeat messages

tldr.problem: When two IPsec peers lose connectivity unexpectedly, they have no way to detect it. SAs (security associations, the encrypted tunnels) can sit idle until they naturally expire, creating a "black hole" where packets are sent into nothing. Large-scale deployments with many tunnels cannot afford to send heartbeat messages regularly to every peer.
tldr.mechanism: Dead Peer Detection (DPD) uses IPsec traffic patterns to detect problems efficiently. If traffic is flowing between peers, that traffic itself proves liveness. Only when the tunnel is idle does a peer send a probe (R-U-THERE, meaning "Are you there?") to check if the peer is still alive. The peer responds with R-U-THERE-ACK. This asynchronous approach scales because most probes are not sent; traffic provides proof of life.
tldr.outcome: Routers and gateways can detect dead peers quickly without the overhead of constant keep-alives. This enables fast failover to backup peers and reclaims IPsec resources. DPD is now widely implemented by major vendors.

today: RFC 3706 is Informational and describes vendor practices that have become widely deployed. DPD is implemented by major IPsec vendors including Cisco, Juniper, and others. It remains the de facto standard for detecting dead IKE peers and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Black Hole Problem
sections.content:
IPsec creates encrypted tunnels between network endpoints. Each tunnel is managed by IKE (Internet Key Exchange), which sets up the security associations that encrypt the traffic. When connectivity is lost unexpectedly—a router reboots, a link fails—the two peers have no way to know. The SAs sit dormant until their lifetimes expire, sometimes hours or days later. During that time, packets are encrypted and sent into the tunnel, but they never arrive. This is a "black hole."

To detect these failures and failover quickly to a backup peer, IPsec systems need a mechanism to prove the other peer is still alive. The challenge is doing this efficiently: in large deployments, a VPN aggregator might manage 50,000 simultaneous tunnels. Sending heartbeat messages to every one every few seconds is computationally expensive and wastes bandwidth.
sections.eli5: A tunnel can break silently. Packets go in and disappear. You need a way to notice fast, but constantly asking "are you alive?" to 50,000 tunnels at once does not scale.

sections.title: Why Traffic Proves Liveness
sections.content:
The key insight behind DPD is that exchanged traffic is proof of liveness. If packets are flowing between two peers, both are clearly alive and connected. A probe is only necessary when the tunnel is idle. If peer A has data to send but has not heard from peer B in a while, it can ask "Are you there?" at that moment, rather than at fixed intervals.

This asynchronous approach reduces the number of probe messages. In a deployment with many idle tunnels, most peers will use their traffic as proof of liveness, and probes are sent only for tunnels that are dormant but about to be used. A peer may define its own "worry metric"—the idle time after which it wants proof. One peer might want quick failover (10 seconds of silence triggers a probe), while another might be content to wait 5 minutes.
sections.eli5: If data is flowing, everything is fine. Only when it is quiet do you check. And you check only when you want to send something new, not on a schedule.

sections.title: The DPD Message Exchange
sections.content:
A DPD exchange is a simple two-message pattern. The sender issues an R-U-THERE (Are You There) Notify message, and the responder answers with R-U-THERE-ACK. The messages are IKE Notify payloads with defined message type numbers (36136 for R-U-THERE, 36137 for R-U-THERE-ACK).

Both messages must be encrypted (the RFC mandates that unencrypted probes be rejected). Each message carries a sequence number so the sender can match the ACK to the probe it sent, detect replays, and know that the peer is genuinely alive and responsive. The sequence number must increment by one with each new R-U-THERE message sent. To guard against spoofing, both peers verify the IKE cookies in the message.

If the sender does not receive an ACK within a timeout, it may retransmit the R-U-THERE message. After a configurable number of failed retransmissions, the implementation should assume the peer is dead and delete the SAs and any related security state.
sections.eli5: One peer asks "Are you there?" with a sequence number. The other answers with the same sequence number. If no answer comes back after a few tries, the peer is dead.

sections.title: DPD Capability and Negotiation
sections.content:
Before DPD exchanges can begin, both peers must advertise that they support DPD. Each peer sends a DPD Vendor ID during IKE Phase 1 negotiation. This Vendor ID is a fixed hash value (with major and minor version numbers) that indicates the peer is DPD-capable. Both peers must send it; if either one does not support DPD, the feature cannot be used.

Importantly, DPD does not require any negotiated parameters. Unlike older keepalive schemes that required peers to agree on a heartbeat interval, DPD is largely independent: each peer can choose its own idle time threshold (its "worry metric") without telling the other peer. The responding peer must understand DPD to answer R-U-THERE messages, but it does not need to initiate probes on the same schedule or at all.
sections.eli5: Both peers say "I can do this" when they set up the tunnel. Then each one can ask questions on its own schedule, no agreement needed.

sections.title: Defending Against Replays and Spoofing
sections.content:
An attacker could intercept a valid R-U-THERE message and flood the responder with copies. The sequence number protects against this: the responder checks that the sequence number matches the incremented sequence number expected from that peer. If an attacker replays an old message with a stale sequence number, the responder will reject it without needing to build and encrypt a response.

The RFC requires both peers to verify the Initiator and Responder cookies in the message's SPI field, ensuring the probe came from the peer's genuine IKE SA and not from an impostor. This, combined with IKE encryption, provides mutual authentication.

Sequence numbers are maintained per peer and per SA. The first R-U-THERE sent in a session should use a random sequence number (with the high bit set to zero to prevent overflow). The high-bit constraint lets sequence numbers increment up to 2 billion before resetting.
sections.eli5: Every probe has a number that increases by one each time. If someone sends the same probe twice, the number does not match what we expected, so we ignore the copy. Fake probes from spoofed IKE sessions also get rejected.

sections.title: Scalability and Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
DPD achieves scalability by reducing per-SA state. Traditional keepalive schemes required two timers per SA: one to signal when to send a HELLO, one to timeout the ACK. Heartbeat schemes also needed two timers. DPD instead maintains a timestamp of the last received traffic. Once an R-U-THERE is sent, a retransmission timer is the only active timer required. This represents a significant reduction in state management, especially when there are tens of thousands of SAs.

An implementation might monitor tunnel idleness and initiate DPD when: (1) an idle period elapses and then the peer needs to send traffic, or (2) the peer has sent outbound IPsec traffic but received nothing back for the idle threshold. The RFC explicitly makes these choices implementation-specific, allowing vendors flexibility in how they trigger probes.

The RFC notes that unlike previous approaches, DPD can even define probes to be sent at regular intervals following an idle period if an implementation prefers that behavior. The key is that probes are not mandated at fixed intervals; the implementation can optimize when and how often they occur.
sections.eli5: Each tunnel does not need two active timers like old systems. A timestamp and maybe a retry timer are enough. Vendors can decide when to check: maybe when the tunnel gets quiet then busy, maybe on a timer only after idle time, whatever scales best.
